At 4940 Eastern Avenue in East Baltimore, on the grounds of Johns Hopkins' Bayview Medical Center campus, this building began operating in May 2015 as the Maryland Advanced Research Computing Center, known as MARCC -- a roughly 3,786-square-foot high-performance computing facility built with $30 million in Maryland state funding as a joint venture between Johns Hopkins University and the University of Maryland, College Park. At launch, MARCC combined more than 19,000 processors and 17 petabytes of storage, connected to partner campuses over fiber-optic links running at 100 gigabits per second, and was already about 80 percent allocated to research users across Johns Hopkins' School of Medicine, Bloomberg School of Public Health, Krieger School of Arts and Sciences, and Whiting School of Engineering, with room designed in for four additional computing modules on the same site.

In August 2021, the university renamed and repositioned the facility as ARCH -- Advanced Research Computing at Hopkins -- reflecting a broader mission beyond the original shared-cluster model. ARCH runs a computing cluster named "Rockfish," funded in part by a National Science Foundation Major Research Instrumentation grant, under a "condo computing" arrangement in which individual research groups purchase their own compute nodes that are integrated into the shared cluster; those groups get priority access to their own hardware plus access to others' unused capacity, with equipment typically refreshed on roughly a five-year cycle. Johns Hopkins describes ARCH as one of the largest academic high-performance computing centers in the country.

Most recently, the Maryland Board of Public Works approved a $9 million state grant on May 6, 2026, toward a roughly 25,000-square-foot expansion of the Bayview data center, incorporating what the university describes as advanced cooling technology intended to reduce energy waste. Notably, a Johns Hopkins spokesperson confirmed the expanded facility's power draw would stay under 10 megawatts -- a figure that keeps it below the threshold set in data-center moratorium legislation introduced weeks earlier by Baltimore City Council President Zeke Cohen and co-sponsored by eleven of the city's fifteen council members, which would pause approval of any data center exceeding that power draw pending a citywide policy review. The expansion is intended to support computing-intensive research spanning life sciences, biomedical research, data science and artificial intelligence, public health, engineering, physics, and astronomy across both the Bayview and Homewood campuses, against a backdrop of separate community pushback over Hopkins' Data Science and AI Institute at Homewood.

reading.body:
ARCH, the Advanced Research Computing at Hopkins facility at Johns Hopkins' Bayview Medical Center campus in East Baltimore, is an academic high-performance computing center that has operated since 2015 and is currently undergoing a state-funded expansion approved in May 2026. The expanded facility will remain under 10 megawatts of power draw, a constraint imposed by the university itself ahead of Baltimore City Council moratorium legislation that would pause approval of data centers exceeding that threshold. At 10 MW, assuming typical academic computing densities of roughly 4 to 5 kW per rack, the facility would house somewhere in the range of 2,000 to 2,500 racks of compute hardware, though no such figure is published by Johns Hopkins.

ARCH serves as an internal cluster called Rockfish under a condo computing model in which research groups at Johns Hopkins' schools of medicine, public health, arts and sciences, and engineering purchase and own their own compute nodes integrated into shared infrastructure, with priority access to their own hardware and access to others' unused capacity. The expansion is explicitly intended to support computing-intensive research in life sciences, biomedical research, data science and artificial intelligence, public health, engineering, physics, and astronomy. No tenant list is published.

Maryland ranks fourth among states where this site has mapped published data center capacity, with 9.3 MW across three facilities reporting power figures. ARCH sits at rank 4 by published megawatts in Maryland. The facility is not a marketed colocation or cloud service and publishes no performance benchmarks, pricing, or grid interconnection details beyond its power cap.
